task_4.title: Document strict_aud support on jwt.decode_complete
task_4.description: Version 2.9.0 clarifies the public API contract for PyJWT by documenting that jwt.decode_complete accepts the strict_aud option. The provided release note points to a docs fix, and the provided production code diff shows no runtime code changes for this item.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the documented jwt.decode_complete API includes the strict_aud option so users can rely on the same advertised decoding options across the library's decode entry points.

expectation.grounded: PyJWT 2.9.0 should present jwt.decode_complete as supporting the strict_aud option in its public API contract. Based on the provided release note and the absence of production code changes in the supplied code diff, this update is a documentation correction rather than a new runtime feature.
expectation.conceptual: Users upgrading to 2.9.0 should be able to discover from the official API surface that complete JWT decoding supports strict audience validation configuration, without implying any newly introduced execution behavior.

constraints.grounded: Do not describe this release item as adding a new decoder path or changing jwt.decode_complete runtime semantics unless separately evidenced. Preserve the existing public API shape and represent this item as documentation alignment for the strict_aud option.
constraints.conceptual: Treat this as a clarification of the published contract, not as a behavioral rewrite. The upgrade should improve discoverability and consistency without introducing unrelated functional changes.

behavior: The jwt.decode_complete API contract includes strict_aud as a supported option in version 2.9.0.
Consumers can interpret strict_aud as applicable when using jwt.decode_complete, rather than assuming the option is unsupported because it was omitted from documentation.
The supplied production code diff does not evidence any runtime logic change associated with this release item.
acceptance_criteria: When a user reviews the 2.9.0 jwt.decode_complete API contract, it should explicitly include strict_aud among the supported options.
When a user compares the documented decoding options across PyJWT decode APIs, jwt.decode_complete should no longer omit strict_aud where it is intended to be available.
The release item should be understood as a documentation clarification and should not imply a newly added runtime capability in the absence of production code changes.

task_3.title: Preserve decode behavior for invalid exp claims during cleanup
task_3.description: Version 2.9.0 includes a small internal cleanup in JWT expiration-claim validation by removing an unnecessary string literal concatenation in the decode error path. The observable contract should remain the same: decoding tokens with a non-integer `exp` claim must still fail with the same error semantics, and normal expiration handling must be unchanged.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.9.0 preserves the existing user-visible behavior for JWT decoding when the `exp` claim is invalid, while incorporating the internal cleanup to the expiration-claim error text construction.

expectation.grounded: During `PyJWT` decode processing, if the payload contains an `exp` claim that cannot be converted to an integer, decoding should raise `DecodeError` for an invalid expiration-time claim. If the `exp` claim is valid but expired relative to current time and leeway handling, decoding should continue to raise `ExpiredSignatureError`.
expectation.conceptual: JWT decoding should continue to reject tokens whose expiration claim is malformed and continue to reject expired tokens using the same public error behavior as before. The 2.9.0 update should not change how callers experience expiration validation failures.

constraints.grounded: Do not alter the public decode API, the use of `DecodeError` for non-integer `exp` values, or the use of `ExpiredSignatureError` for expired tokens. Do not change expiration comparison semantics involving current time and leeway.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should be behaviorally neutral aside from code cleanup. Invalid expiration data must still fail in the same way, and valid expiration checks must behave exactly as before.

behavior: When decoding a JWT payload with an `exp` claim that is present but not coercible to an integer, the library raises `DecodeError` instead of treating the claim as valid.
When decoding a JWT payload with an integer `exp` claim that is at or before the effective expiration threshold after applying leeway, the library raises `ExpiredSignatureError`.
The 2.9.0 change is limited to cleanup of error text construction and does not introduce a new API, new validation branch, or different expiration decision logic.
acceptance_criteria: When a token is decoded and its `exp` claim is a non-integer value, decoding should fail with `DecodeError` for an invalid expiration claim.
When a token is decoded and its `exp` claim is a valid integer but the token is expired after applying leeway rules, decoding should fail with `ExpiredSignatureError`.
When upgrading from 2.8.0 to 2.9.0, callers relying on expiration validation outcomes should observe no behavioral regression in decode success or failure decisions.

task_2.title: Support multiple allowed JWT issuers during validation
task_2.description: The 2.9.0 update expands JWT issuer validation so callers can provide either a single allowed issuer or a list of allowed issuers. Validation should continue to reject tokens whose issuer claim does not match any allowed value, while preserving existing missing-claim and single-issuer behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWT issuer validation accepts either one issuer value or multiple allowed issuer values, so tokens with an `iss` claim matching any configured allowed issuer are treated as valid while non-matching or missing issuer claims continue to fail validation appropriately.

expectation.grounded: Any public JWT validation API that accepts an `issuer` parameter must support either a single string or a `List[str]`. If the token `iss` claim equals the provided string, validation succeeds as before. If `issuer` is a list of strings, validation succeeds when the token `iss` claim matches one of the listed values and raises `InvalidIssuerError` when it does not. If issuer validation is requested and the token has no `iss` claim, `MissingRequiredClaimError` must still be raised. Existing method signatures remain unchanged apart from broader accepted typing for `issuer`.
expectation.conceptual: Issuer validation should allow applications to configure one trusted issuer or several trusted issuers without changing how they call the library. Tokens should be accepted when their issuer matches any configured allowed issuer, rejected when the issuer does not match, and still rejected when issuer validation is required but the issuer claim is absent.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress the existing single-string issuer validation path. Keep the observable failure mode for issuer mismatches as `InvalidIssuerError` and preserve missing-issuer handling as `MissingRequiredClaimError`. Treat list-based validation as an exact membership check against the token `iss` claim; this change only broadens accepted `issuer` input from one string to a list of strings.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should add multi-issuer support without changing established behavior for current single-issuer consumers. Error outcomes for missing or invalid issuers must remain consistent, and the new behavior should only expand which issuer configurations are accepted.

behavior: JWT issuer validation accepts an `issuer` configuration supplied as either a single string or a list of strings.
When a single issuer string is provided, validation behavior remains unchanged and succeeds only on an exact match with the token `iss` claim.
When a list of issuer strings is provided, validation succeeds if the token `iss` claim matches any entry in the list.
When the token `iss` claim does not match the configured issuer string or any configured issuer in the list, validation raises `InvalidIssuerError`.
When issuer validation is requested but the token does not contain an `iss` claim, validation raises `MissingRequiredClaimError`.
acceptance_criteria: When issuer validation is performed with a single allowed issuer string and the token `iss` claim exactly matches it, the token should be accepted.
When issuer validation is performed with a single allowed issuer string and the token `iss` claim differs, validation should raise `InvalidIssuerError`.
When issuer validation is performed with a list of allowed issuer strings and the token `iss` claim matches one of them, the token should be accepted.
When issuer validation is performed with a list of allowed issuer strings and the token `iss` claim matches none of them, validation should raise `InvalidIssuerError`.

When issuer validation is requested and the token lacks an `iss` claim, validation should raise `MissingRequiredClaimError` regardless of whether the configured allowed issuer input is a string or a list.

task_1.title: Raise the Python baseline to 3.8 and support Python 3.12
task_1.description: Version 2.9.0 updates runtime compatibility by dropping Python 3.7 support and adding Python 3.12 support, while keeping the existing JWT feature surface intact for supported Python versions.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that version 2.9.0 is treated as a runtime-compatibility upgrade: the library must support Python 3.12, stop claiming support for Python 3.7, and preserve the existing JWT API behavior for users on supported Python versions.

expectation.grounded: The package should support Python 3.12 and require Python 3.8 or newer. In `jwt.algorithms`, compatibility should align with Python 3.8+ by relying on the standard-library `typing.Literal` rather than a Python 3.7 fallback, and the cryptography-backed algorithm layer should remain compatible with cryptography exception surfaces that include `UnsupportedAlgorithm` and `InvalidSignature`.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should refresh interpreter compatibility boundaries without changing how users normally call the JWT APIs. Users on current Python releases should be able to adopt 2.9.0, while Python 3.7 users should understand that this version is no longer for their runtime.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce a new JWT encoding, decoding, or algorithm-selection API as part of this upgrade. Existing behavior for supported runtimes should remain stable aside from the supported-Python-version contract and compatibility with current cryptography exception definitions.
constraints.conceptual: This change is about supported environments, not a redesign of JWT behavior. Supported users should see continuity in everyday library behavior, and unsupported runtimes should simply fall outside the version's compatibility promise.

behavior: Version 2.9.0 supports Python 3.12 as a valid runtime target.
Python 3.7 is no longer part of the supported runtime matrix; Python 3.8+ becomes the effective baseline.
The algorithms layer aligns with Python 3.8+ typing behavior instead of maintaining a Python 3.7 typing compatibility path.
Cryptography-backed algorithm handling remains compatible with cryptography environments that expose `UnsupportedAlgorithm` alongside `InvalidSignature`.
acceptance_criteria: When users run version 2.9.0 on Python 3.12, the library should be considered supported and its normal JWT functionality should remain available.
When users evaluate runtime compatibility for version 2.9.0, Python 3.7 should be treated as unsupported and Python 3.8 or newer as supported.
When existing applications upgrade from 2.8.0 to 2.9.0 on a supported Python version, they should not need to change their normal JWT encode, decode, or algorithm usage solely because of this update.
When the library interacts with supported cryptography backends on supported Python versions, its algorithm support handling should remain compatible with the current cryptography exception surface.

task_6.title: Clarify JWKS example by removing unused variable
task_6.description: Version 2.9.0 clarifies the documented example for retrieving RSA signing keys from a JWKS endpoint by removing an unused variable. The change reduces confusion about which values are actually needed, without altering library runtime behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the published example for retrieving RSA signing keys from a JWKS endpoint only includes variables that are actually used, so users are not misled into thinking an unused `kid` value is required.

expectation.grounded: The 2.9.0 update should revise the example titled "Retrieve RSA signing keys from a JWKS endpoint" so it no longer declares an unused `kid` variable. This upgrade item is documentation-only and does not introduce any public API, runtime, or error-handling changes.
expectation.conceptual: The JWKS usage example should reflect only the inputs that matter to the documented flow. Users reading the example should not see extra values that imply a requirement or step that does not affect behavior.

constraints.grounded: Do not change runtime behavior, return values, raised errors, or public interfaces as part of this update item. Keep the scope limited to clarifying the example content described in the release note.
constraints.conceptual: This update should improve clarity only. Existing library behavior and integration semantics should remain unchanged.

behavior: The documented JWKS example for retrieving RSA signing keys should no longer include an unused `kid` variable.
Users following the example should no longer be given the impression that `kid` must be separately defined when it is not used in the illustrated flow.
This upgrade item does not change production runtime behavior in the library.
acceptance_criteria: When a user reads the example for retrieving RSA signing keys from a JWKS endpoint, it should include only variables that are actually used in the demonstrated flow.
When comparing the 2.9.0 example to the prior version, the unused `kid` variable should be absent.
When upgrading from 2.8.0 to 2.9.0 for this item alone, application runtime behavior should remain unchanged.

task_5.title: Treat 2.9.0 as a documentation-only release
task_5.description: Version 2.9.0 is represented by a release note that only references a documentation-step fix. With no accompanying code diff, the upgrade should be understood as documentation maintenance rather than a runtime, API, or behavior change.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading from 2.8.0 to 2.9.0 is treated as a documentation-only release and does not imply any runtime, API, or integration behavior change for library consumers.

expectation.grounded: The 2.9.0 release note identifies a docs-step fix. Because no code changes are evidenced in the provided code diff, the upgrade should expose no new runtime features, no changed public API behavior, and no new observable warnings or errors during normal library use.
expectation.conceptual: Users upgrading to 2.9.0 should experience the same library behavior as in 2.8.0. The release only corrects documentation-related maintenance and should not affect application behavior.

constraints.grounded: Do not characterize this upgrade as adding functionality, changing signatures, altering runtime semantics, or introducing compatibility breaks. The absence of code-diff evidence should be preserved as a no-runtime-change boundary.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must remain non-disruptive for existing consumers and should not require application code changes.

behavior: Version 2.9.0 is classified as a documentation-maintenance release rather than a functional library update.
No public runtime behavior changes are evidenced by the provided materials.
No new public API surface, deprecation, or breaking compatibility change is evidenced by the provided materials.
acceptance_criteria: When a consumer evaluates the upgrade from 2.8.0 to 2.9.0, it should be classified as documentation-only rather than a runtime feature or fix.
When an existing integration upgrades to 2.9.0, it should not need application code changes because no runtime-facing behavior change is specified.
When release notes are summarized for users, the change should be described as a documentation-step correction with unchanged library behavior.

task_7.title: Add Python 3.12 support and drop Python 3.7 support
task_7.description: The upgrade to 2.9.0 expands the library's supported Python runtime matrix to include Python 3.12 and removes Python 3.7 support. The public JWT APIs remain the same for supported environments, while the algorithms module is aligned with Python 3.8+ typing and newer cryptography-backed runtime combinations.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to version 2.9.0 supports running the library on Python 3.12 while no longer treating Python 3.7 as a supported runtime, without changing the normal user-facing JWT encode, decode, and algorithm usage on supported Python versions.

expectation.grounded: PyJWT 2.9.0 should support importing and using `jwt.algorithms` on Python 3.12 and other supported interpreters by relying on the standard-library `typing.Literal` path used in Python 3.8+ environments. Python 3.7 is out of support for this release. Public JWT APIs and cryptography-backed algorithm availability should remain consistent for supported runtimes.
expectation.conceptual: After the upgrade, applications using the library should be able to run on Python 3.12 with the same normal JWT workflows they used before, while environments pinned to Python 3.7 should be considered unsupported and expected to upgrade their interpreter.

constraints.grounded: Do not introduce new user-facing JWT API requirements for supported environments beyond the interpreter support change. Existing `jwt` encode/decode flows and supported algorithm access should continue to work on supported Python versions. The release should not imply continued compatibility guarantees for Python 3.7.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should behave as a compatibility expansion for current supported users, not as a functional redesign. The only breaking boundary exposed to users is the supported Python version range.

behavior: Python 3.12 is a supported runtime for the upgraded library version.
Python 3.7 is no longer a supported runtime for this release.
The algorithms module now assumes a Python 3.8+ typing environment rather than a compatibility fallback for older interpreters.
For supported Python versions, existing JWT encoding, decoding, and algorithm-selection behavior remains intended to stay stable across the upgrade.
acceptance_criteria: When an application upgrades to version 2.9.0 and runs on Python 3.12, it should be able to import and use the library's normal JWT APIs successfully.
When an application remains on a supported interpreter version in the Python 3.8+ range, upgrading should not require changing standard `jwt` encode or decode usage solely because of this release.
When evaluating supported environments for version 2.9.0, Python 3.7 should no longer be counted as supported.

When consumers use algorithm functionality through the library on supported interpreters, they should observe compatibility with the existing public API surface rather than a renamed or redesigned JWT workflow.

task_8.title: Tighten and speed up SSH key detection
task_8.description: PyJWT 2.9.0 changes SSH key detection so `jwt.utils.is_ssh_key` identifies supported SSH public keys from their leading key-type prefix instead of searching for those markers anywhere in the input. This improves runtime efficiency and makes detection stricter by avoiding accidental substring matches while preserving recognition of supported SSH key prefixes.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that SSH key detection recognizes only supported SSH public keys whose data begins with a valid SSH key type marker, so key classification is faster and does not misidentify unrelated byte strings that merely contain SSH key text later in the input.

expectation.grounded: The public helper `jwt.utils.is_ssh_key(key: bytes)` should return `True` only when `key` starts with one of the supported SSH key type prefixes: `ssh-ed25519`, `ssh-rsa`, `ssh-dss`, `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`, `ecdsa-sha2-nistp384`, or `ecdsa-sha2-nistp521`. It should return `False` for inputs that do not begin with one of those prefixes, even if one of the same tokens appears later in the byte string. Inputs that begin with a supported base type and continue as OpenSSH certificate-style key identifiers should still be treated as SSH keys.
expectation.conceptual: SSH key detection should rely on the declared key type at the start of the key data. Supported SSH public keys, including supported certificate-style variants that begin with those key types, should still be recognized, while unrelated data should not be accepted just because it contains similar text somewhere inside.

constraints.grounded: Do not expand support beyond the existing six SSH key type families. Preserve the boolean return behavior of `jwt.utils.is_ssh_key` and maintain compatibility for supported SSH public key prefixes without introducing new APIs, warnings, or alternate result types.
constraints.conceptual: Keep the change limited to stricter and faster recognition of already supported SSH public key formats. Existing valid SSH key inputs should remain accepted, and the upgrade should not require callers to adopt a new interface.

behavior: `jwt.utils.is_ssh_key` classifies SSH keys by checking whether the byte string begins with one of the supported SSH key type prefixes.
Inputs that contain supported SSH key type text only later in the byte string are no longer classified as SSH keys.
OpenSSH certificate-style public key identifiers that start with a supported base SSH key type continue to be classified as SSH keys.
SSH key detection avoids scanning the full input for matching substrings, reducing overhead during key-format identification.
acceptance_criteria: When `jwt.utils.is_ssh_key` receives bytes beginning with `ssh-ed25519`, `ssh-rsa`, `ssh-dss`, `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`, `ecdsa-sha2-nistp384`, or `ecdsa-sha2-nistp521`, it should return `True`.
When `jwt.utils.is_ssh_key` receives bytes that do not begin with a supported SSH key type prefix, it should return `False`.
When a supported SSH key type token appears only after the beginning of the byte string, the input should not be treated as an SSH key.
When an OpenSSH certificate-style public key begins with a supported base SSH key type, it should still be treated as an SSH key.

task_9.title: Support decoding directly with PyJWK keys
task_9.description: The upgrade makes JWT decoding accept a `PyJWK` object directly instead of requiring callers to extract its raw key first. When a `PyJWK` is used, decoding can safely infer the allowed algorithm from the JWK itself, while still rejecting algorithm mismatches and surfacing missing cryptography support with a more specific error during JWK creation.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that decoding accepts a `PyJWK` object as the verification key, automatically uses the JWK's own algorithm when callers do not provide `algorithms`, and preserves safe algorithm validation and dependency-related failures.

expectation.grounded: When `jwt.decode()` or the underlying JWS decode flow receives a `PyJWK` as `key`, it should accept that object directly instead of requiring `PyJWK.key`. If signature verification is enabled and `algorithms` is omitted for a `PyJWK`, the allowed algorithms should default to the JWK's resolved algorithm name exposed on the `PyJWK`. Verification should use the `PyJWK`'s resolved algorithm object and prepared key material, and a token whose header `alg` does not match the allowed set should still raise `InvalidAlgorithmError`. Creating a `PyJWK` for an algorithm that requires `cryptography` should raise `MissingCryptographyError` when that dependency is unavailable.
expectation.conceptual: Callers should be able to pass a JWK wrapper directly into decode without manually unpacking it. If that wrapper already defines the signing algorithm, decode should use that algorithm by default, while still rejecting tokens signed with a different algorithm and reporting missing crypto support through the specific dependency error.

constraints.grounded: Continue requiring an explicit `algorithms` argument for non-`PyJWK` decode keys when signature verification is enabled. Do not broaden accepted algorithms beyond the caller-provided list or the `PyJWK`'s own algorithm when inference is used. Keep existing signature verification and invalid-algorithm failure behavior for mismatched or unsupported token algorithms.
constraints.conceptual: Only relax the missing-`algorithms` requirement when the key itself already carries authoritative algorithm metadata. Preserve existing decode safety rules and continue failing closed on mismatched, unsupported, or unverifiable signatures.

behavior: `PyJWK` instances expose their resolved algorithm name for use during decode.
Decode accepts a `PyJWK` object anywhere a verification key is accepted.
When a `PyJWK` is passed and `algorithms` is omitted, decode infers the allowed algorithm from the JWK instead of failing solely because `algorithms` was not provided.
Verification with a `PyJWK` uses the JWK's resolved algorithm implementation and prepared key directly.
If the token header algorithm is not allowed, including when it differs from an inferred `PyJWK` algorithm, decode raises `InvalidAlgorithmError`.
If a `PyJWK` targets an algorithm that requires the `cryptography` dependency and that dependency is unavailable, JWK construction raises `MissingCryptographyError`.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller passes a valid `PyJWK` whose algorithm matches the token, decode should succeed without requiring the caller to extract the wrapped key first.
When a caller passes a valid `PyJWK` and omits `algorithms`, decode should still verify the token by using the algorithm declared by the JWK.
When a caller passes a `PyJWK` whose declared algorithm does not match the token header algorithm, decode should fail with `InvalidAlgorithmError`.
When a caller passes a non-`PyJWK` key and omits `algorithms` while signature verification is enabled, decode should continue to reject the call.
When a caller constructs a `PyJWK` for an algorithm that depends on `cryptography` in an environment where that dependency is not installed, the library should raise `MissingCryptographyError`.

task_10.title: Expose the resolved JWK algorithm on PyJWK
task_10.description: The upgrade makes parsed JWK objects expose their resolved algorithm name so callers can reuse it in downstream JWT operations, and it surfaces a dedicated missing-dependency error when a JWK algorithm requires cryptography support that is not installed.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications using PyJWK can read the resolved algorithm directly from the parsed JWK object and receive a specific dependency error when constructing a PyJWK for an algorithm that requires cryptography support.

expectation.grounded: A successful `PyJWK` created through the constructor, `PyJWK.from_dict()`, or `PyJWK.from_json()` should expose the resolved algorithm string via `algorithm_name`, alongside the existing `Algorithm` and `key` outputs. If the resolved algorithm requires `cryptography` and that dependency is unavailable, PyJWK construction should raise `MissingCryptographyError` instead of the generic `PyJWKError`.
expectation.conceptual: Parsed JWK objects should carry their own algorithm identifier so callers can use the same algorithm consistently in later JWT operations. Missing optional crypto support should fail with a dependency-specific error rather than a generic JWK failure.

constraints.grounded: Existing successful key parsing behavior must remain intact: supported algorithms should still resolve to the same `Algorithm` implementation and produce the same `key`, while unsupported or unresolvable algorithms must still fail with `PyJWKError`. The exposed `algorithm_name` must match the algorithm actually selected for the `PyJWK` instance.
constraints.conceptual: This change should add algorithm introspection and clearer dependency failures without weakening existing validation. Valid JWKs should continue to parse normally, and invalid or unsupported algorithms should still be rejected.

behavior: A successfully constructed `PyJWK` now exposes the resolved algorithm identifier through the public `algorithm_name` attribute.
The value of `algorithm_name` reflects the algorithm selected for that JWK instance, including cases where the algorithm is inferred from the JWK data or provided explicitly by the caller.
When the selected JWK algorithm depends on `cryptography` and that dependency is not installed, constructing `PyJWK` raises `MissingCryptographyError`.
If the selected algorithm cannot be mapped to a supported JWK algorithm implementation, constructing `PyJWK` continues to raise `PyJWKError`.
acceptance_criteria: When a JWK is successfully parsed into `PyJWK`, the resulting object should expose its resolved algorithm through `algorithm_name`.
When a caller explicitly provides an algorithm while creating `PyJWK`, `algorithm_name` should report that selected algorithm after successful construction.
When a supported JWK is parsed successfully, the existing `Algorithm` and `key` behaviors should remain available in addition to `algorithm_name`.
When a JWK selects an algorithm that requires `cryptography` but the dependency is unavailable, creating `PyJWK` should fail with `MissingCryptographyError`.
When a JWK selects an unsupported or unresolvable algorithm, creating `PyJWK` should still fail with `PyJWKError`.

task_11.title: Normalize invalid RSA PEM key parsing errors for cryptography 42 compatibility
task_11.description: The upgrade changes RSA PEM key handling so invalid or unsupported public key material is reported through the library's InvalidKeyError interface instead of exposing lower-level parsing exceptions. This keeps RSA key validation behavior consistent for users upgrading alongside newer cryptography releases.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that RSA PEM key parsing remains compatible with newer cryptography releases by surfacing invalid public key input as the library's InvalidKeyError instead of leaking backend parsing exceptions.

expectation.grounded: When RSAAlgorithm.prepare_key processes PEM-encoded RSA key input and private-key parsing falls back to public-key parsing, any public-key parse failure caused by invalid PEM content or an unsupported public key format must raise InvalidKeyError. Valid RSA private and public PEM keys must continue to be accepted without changing their successful behavior.
expectation.conceptual: Applications using RSA key input should receive one consistent library-level invalid-key failure when the supplied PEM data cannot be parsed as a supported RSA key, including under newer cryptography versions. Valid RSA PEM keys should keep working as before.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the successful handling of supported RSA private keys or RSA public keys. Do not expose ValueError or UnsupportedAlgorithm from the public key parsing path when the input is invalid or unsupported; normalize those failures to InvalidKeyError instead.
constraints.conceptual: The change should be limited to error normalization for bad RSA PEM input and must not alter normal behavior for valid keys or broaden the visible exception surface for callers.

behavior: RSA PEM key preparation continues to attempt RSA private key parsing before falling back to RSA public key parsing.
If the fallback RSA public key parse fails because the PEM data is invalid, the observable failure becomes InvalidKeyError.
If the fallback RSA public key parse fails because the key format is unsupported by the cryptography backend, the observable failure becomes InvalidKeyError.
This compatibility behavior applies when using newer cryptography releases that may raise UnsupportedAlgorithm during PEM public key loading.
acceptance_criteria: When an application passes a valid RSA private PEM key to RSAAlgorithm.prepare_key, it should still return a usable RSA private key object.
When an application passes a valid RSA public PEM key to RSAAlgorithm.prepare_key, it should still return a usable RSA public key object.
When an application passes invalid PEM content that cannot be parsed as an RSA public key, RSAAlgorithm.prepare_key should raise InvalidKeyError.

When an application passes PEM key content that reaches public-key parsing but is rejected by the cryptography backend as an unsupported algorithm or format, RSAAlgorithm.prepare_key should raise InvalidKeyError instead of exposing the backend exception.

task_12.title: Expose missing cryptography dependency during JWK loading
task_12.description: PyJWT 2.9.0 now fails fast with a dedicated JWK error when JWK processing requires the optional cryptography backend but that dependency is not installed, instead of masking the problem as a generic JWK issue or silently skipping the affected key in a JWK set.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWK and JWK set loading surfaces a clear runtime failure when the selected key algorithm requires the optional cryptography dependency and that dependency is missing, rather than hiding the misconfiguration behind a generic JWK error or by skipping the key.

expectation.grounded: When `PyJWK` is created for a JWK whose resolved algorithm is in the set of algorithms that require `cryptography`, and the cryptography backend is unavailable, it must raise `MissingCryptographyError`. `MissingCryptographyError` must be a `PyJWKError` subtype. When `PyJWKSet` loads keys and encounters that condition, it must propagate `MissingCryptographyError` instead of swallowing it as an unusable-key case.
expectation.conceptual: If application code loads JWT key material that depends on crypto support not present in the runtime environment, the library should fail immediately with a specific missing-dependency error so the deployment issue is obvious and the key set is not partially accepted.

constraints.grounded: Existing JWK validation behavior for unsupported key types, unknown algorithms, malformed JWK data, and other non-dependency-related failures should remain under the existing JWK error model. `PyJWKSet` should continue skipping keys that are otherwise unusable for reasons other than missing cryptography support.
constraints.conceptual: Do not broaden this change beyond the missing dependency case. Normal invalid-key handling should stay consistent, and only absent crypto support should become a hard stop during JWK set loading.

behavior: A dedicated `MissingCryptographyError` is exposed for JWK-related failures caused by the optional `cryptography` dependency being unavailable.
Creating a `PyJWK` for an algorithm that requires cryptography now raises `MissingCryptographyError` instead of a generic `PyJWKError` when that dependency is missing.
Building a `PyJWKSet` no longer suppresses missing-cryptography failures by treating the affected key as merely unusable; it re-raises the missing-dependency error.
Other JWK set entries that fail for unrelated `PyJWTError` reasons remain skippable during JWK set construction.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller creates `PyJWK` from JWK data that resolves to an algorithm requiring cryptography in an environment where `cryptography` is not installed, it should raise `MissingCryptographyError`.

When a caller creates `PyJWKSet` containing at least one key that requires cryptography in an environment where `cryptography` is not installed, it should fail with `MissingCryptographyError` instead of silently omitting that key.

When `PyJWKSet` encounters keys that are unusable for reasons other than a missing cryptography dependency, it should continue its existing behavior for non-loadable keys without turning every such failure into a hard dependency error.
When JWK input is invalid for unrelated reasons, callers should continue to observe the established JWK error categories rather than the new missing-dependency error.
